    Integrating fast frequentist empirical-Bayes gene-expression dispersion estimation as a prior

    Stefano Mangiola

    Source: vignettes/dispersion-priors.Rmd
    dispersion-priors.Rmd

    brmDE, although very flexible, capable of mixed-effect models, native non-parametric smooth/spline models, and alternative distributions (NB and ZINB), fits one gene at a time to prioritise parallelisation. A single-gene likelihood cannot borrow strength across features, which is exactly what makes a feature-wise negative-binomial dispersion useful when there are small numbers of replicates.

    Frequentist methods estimate gene-wise dispersion through empirical Bayes very efficiently, although only for relatively simple fixed-effect models.

    The key idea is to cheaply estimate gene dispersion with empirical Bayes, for example through edgeR or DESeq2, and use it as an approximate prior for brmDE. With enough evidence from the data, the gene’s own counts can still pull the posterior away from the upstream empirical-Bayes estimate.

    Using empirical-Bayes dispersion estimation as prior

    brmDE offers two priors for the (zero-inflated) negative-binomial dispersion.

    Empirical-Bayes methods such as edgeR estimate a negative-binomial dispersion trend across genes, a moderated gene-wise dispersion, and a prior degrees of freedom that controls the strength of the gene-wise shrinkage.

    For a gene gg, we denote:

    • ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} as edgeR’s trended.dispersion, the negative-binomial dispersion expected for a gene with that abundance;
    • ϕtagwise,g\phi_{\mathrm{tagwise},g} as edgeR’s tagwise.dispersion, the gene-specific negative-binomial dispersion after empirical-Bayes shrinkage;
    • d0d_0 as edgeR’s prior.df, which measures the strength of the across-gene information used for shrinkage.

    brmDE uses ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} and d0d_0 to construct a Bayesian prior. The tagwise dispersion is not used as the prior location because it already contains gene-specific information from the same data that will subsequently be fitted by brmDE.

    Importantly, edgeR does not place a conjugate scaled-inverse-chi-square prior directly on the negative-binomial dispersion ϕg\phi_g. Its tagwise negative-binomial dispersions are obtained using weighted likelihood. The Gamma construction below is therefore a brmDE approximation that translates edgeR’s dispersion trend and empirically estimated shrinkage strength into a conventional Bayesian prior.

    Gamma prior

    edgeR provides two quantities that are useful for constructing a prior on the negative-binomial dispersion:

    ϕtrend,g \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}

    the expected negative-binomial dispersion for a gene with the abundance of gene gg, and

    d0 d_0

    the prior degrees of freedom, which quantifies the strength of the across-gene shrinkage information.

    edgeR does not define a conjugate scaled-inverse-chi-square prior directly on ϕg\phi_g. To translate these two quantities into a Bayesian prior, brmDE uses the following approximation:

    ϕgtrue∼brmDEϕtrend,gd0χd02. \phi_g^{true} \overset{\mathrm{brmDE}}{\sim} \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} \frac{d_0}{\chi^2_{d_0}}.

    This construction has the desired properties: the prior is centred according to the abundance-dependent edgeR dispersion trend, while d0d_0 controls its concentration. A large d0d_0 produces a narrow distribution around the trend, whereas a small d0d_0 produces a wider prior.

    brms parameterises the negative binomial by the precision-like parameter shape, which is the reciprocal of the edgeR dispersion:

    shape=1ϕgtrue. \mathrm{shape} = \frac{1}{\phi_g^{true}}.

    Under the brmDE approximation,

    shape=χd02d0ϕtrend,g. \mathrm{shape} = \frac{\chi^2_{d_0}} {d_0\,\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}}.

    A chi-square distribution is a special case of the Gamma distribution,

    χd2≡Gamma(d2,scale=2), \chi^2_d \equiv \mathrm{Gamma}\left( \frac{d}{2}, \mathrm{scale}=2 \right),

    and multiplying a Gamma-distributed variable by a positive constant produces another Gamma distribution. Therefore,

    shape∼Gamma(d02,scale=2d0ϕtrend,g), \mathrm{shape} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\left( \frac{d_0}{2}, \mathrm{scale} = \frac{2} {d_0\,\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}} \right),

    or equivalently,

    shape∼Gamma(d02,rate=d0ϕtrend,g2). \boxed{ \mathrm{shape} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\left( \frac{d_0}{2}, \mathrm{rate} = \frac{d_0\,\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}}{2} \right). }

    Quantity Interpretation As a Gamma
    χd02\chi^2_{d_0} chi-square random variable Gamma(d0/2,scale=2)\mathrm{Gamma}(d_0/2,\ \mathrm{scale}=2)
    ϕgtrue\phi_g^{true} brmDE scaled-inverse-chi-square approximation to the true NB dispersion inverse-Gamma(d0/2,scale=d0ϕtrend,g/2)(d_0/2,\ \mathrm{scale}=d_0\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}/2)
    1/ϕgtrue=shape1/\phi_g^{true}=\mathrm{shape} reciprocal NB dispersion Gamma(d0/2,rate=d0ϕtrend,g/2)\mathrm{Gamma}(d_0/2,\ \mathrm{rate}=d_0\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}/2)
    exp⁡(b0)=shape×ϕtrend,g\exp(b_0)=\mathrm{shape}\times\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} multiplicative deviation from the trend Gamma(d0/2,rate=d0/2)\mathrm{Gamma}(d_0/2,\ \mathrm{rate}=d_0/2)

    Simplifying the prior further: using ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} as offset

    brms puts shape behind a log link, so

    shape ~ 1 + offset(log(1/dispersion_trended))

    corresponds to

    log⁡(shape)=b0+log⁡(1/ϕtrend,g). \log(\mathrm{shape}) = b_0 + \log(1/\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}).

    The intercept is therefore the log multiplicative deviation from the edgeR trend:

    b0=log⁡(shape)−log⁡(1/ϕtrend,g)=log⁡(shape×ϕtrend,g). b_0 = \log(\mathrm{shape}) - \log(1/\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}) = \log( \mathrm{shape}\times\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} ).

    Exponentiating gives

    exp⁡(b0)=shape×ϕtrend,g. \exp(b_0) = \mathrm{shape}\times\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}.

    Under the Gamma approximation derived above,

    exp⁡(b0)∼Gamma(d02,rate=d02). \boxed{ \exp(b_0) \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\left( \frac{d_0}{2}, \mathrm{rate} = \frac{d_0}{2} \right). }

    The resulting prior is the same for every gene on the multiplicative-deviation scale. Gene-specific abundance information enters through the offset ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}, while d0d_0 determines the concentration of the prior.

    The trailing + Intercept_shape is the log-Jacobian of the exponential transformation. Without it, the density would be misnormalised on the log scale and would no longer correspond to the Gamma distribution derived above. Both parameters arrive as data rather than literals, allowing the generated Stan code to remain identical across genes and the compiled model to be reused.

    The Student-t prior (default)

    The Gamma prior provides a direct Bayesian approximation based on edgeR’s negative-binomial dispersion trend and empirical-Bayes shrinkage strength. Its relatively thin tails, however, can make the upstream edgeR information influential when the brmDE model differs substantially from the fixed-effect negative-binomial model used to estimate that information.

    There are two important situations in which the edgeR dispersion trend can be systematically displaced from the dispersion estimated by brmDE (see Appendix 1).

    • Because edgeR dispersion estimation cannot fit mixed-effects models, a mixed-effects brmDE model must be approximated by a fixed-effects model. For example, ~ treatment + (1 | hospital) may be approximated by ~ treatment + hospital. The fixed effects are estimated without partial pooling and can absorb more variation, potentially reducing the residual negative-binomial dispersion.

    • A zero-inflated negative-binomial model in brmDE must be approximated upstream by an ordinary negative-binomial model. Zero inflation can then be absorbed by the edgeR negative-binomial dispersion, potentially increasing the estimated dispersion.

    For these cases, brmDE provides a heavy-tailed Student-t alternative that uses the same edgeR trend as its prior location while allowing the gene’s likelihood to move substantially further from it.

    Simplifying the prior like for gamma: using ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} as offset

    The submodel is the one already assembled above. On

    shape ~ 1 + offset(log(1/dispersion_trended))

    the intercept has a Student-t prior, student_t(ν, 0, σ). The Gamma alternative puts Gamma(d0/2,d0/2)\mathrm{Gamma}(d_0/2,\; d_0/2) on exp⁡(b0)\exp(b_0) instead. The offset is the same; only the intercept prior changes.

    From d0d_0 to a log-scale SD

    The Student-t prior uses the same edgeR-derived shrinkage strength as the Gamma approximation, but replaces the thin-tailed Gamma-derived distribution with a heavy-tailed distribution on the log scale.

    Under the reference Gamma approximation,

    exp⁡(b0)∼Gamma(d02,rate=d02). \exp(b_0) \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\left( \frac{d_0}{2}, \mathrm{rate} = \frac{d_0}{2} \right).

    The variance of the logarithm of a Gamma random variable depends only on its shape parameter. For

    X∼Gamma(a,⋅), X\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(a,\cdot),

    Var(log⁡X)=ψ′(a), \mathrm{Var}(\log X) = \psi'(a),

    where ψ′\psi' is the trigamma function.

    Using a=d0/2a=d_0/2, the log-scale standard deviation of the reference Gamma prior is therefore

    SD(b0)=ψ′(d0/2). \boxed{ \mathrm{SD}(b_0) = \sqrt{\psi'(d_0/2)}. }

    brmDE uses this standard deviation to calibrate the width of the Student-t prior. This is a deliberate variance-matching approximation: d0d_0 comes from edgeR’s empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimation, while the Student-t distribution supplies heavier tails than the reference Gamma prior.

    From SD to the Student-t scale

    brms writes student_t(ν, μ, σ) with a scale, not a standard deviation. For ν>2\nu > 2,

    SD=σνν−2,soσ=SDν−2ν. \mathrm{SD} = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\nu-2}}, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \sigma = \mathrm{SD}\sqrt{\frac{\nu-2}{\nu}}.

    At the default ν=3\nu=3,

    σ=SD/3. \sigma = \mathrm{SD}/\sqrt{3}.

    Putting both steps together, at the default ν=3\nu=3,

    SD(b0)=ψ′(d0/2),σ=SD(b0)ν−2ν=ψ′(d0/2)3. \mathrm{SD}(b_0) = \sqrt{\psi'(d_0/2)}, \qquad \sigma = \mathrm{SD}(b_0)\sqrt{\frac{\nu-2}{\nu}} = \frac{\sqrt{\psi'(d_0/2)}}{\sqrt{3}}.

    Appendix 1: Background on empirical-Bayes estimation of dispersion in edgeR

    The negative-binomial dispersion used as the brmDE prior location and the quasi-likelihood dispersion used internally to estimate shrinkage strength are distinct quantities.

    For the negative-binomial model, edgeR estimates an abundance-dependent trend

    ϕtrend,g, \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g},

    and gene-specific tagwise negative-binomial dispersions

    ϕtagwise,g. \phi_{\mathrm{tagwise},g}.

    The tagwise estimates are obtained by weighted-likelihood empirical Bayes rather than through a conjugate inverse-chi-square prior.

    However, estimateDisp() also needs to determine how strongly gene-specific dispersions should be shrunk towards the trend. The returned prior.df, denoted d0d_0, is estimated using residual quasi-likelihood variance machinery closely related to the empirical-Bayes framework used by limma.

    This appendix describes that calculation.

    Sampling uncertainty of a variance estimate

    The connection between variance uncertainty and degrees of freedom comes from the classical sampling distribution of a sample variance. For normally distributed observations,

    ds2σ2∼χd2, \frac{d\,s^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_d,

    where:

    • s2s^2 is the variance estimated from the observed sample;
    • σ2\sigma^2 is the unknown true population variance;
    • dd is the residual degrees of freedom. For nn observations described only by their mean, d=n−1d=n-1.

    The sample variance itself is not chi-square distributed. Its ratio to the true variance, after multiplication by its degrees of freedom, follows a chi-square distribution.

    edgeR applies the same variance-moderation principle to a residual quasi-likelihood dispersion. Using simplified notation,

    dqgresidualqgtrue∼χd2. \frac{d\,q_g^{residual}} {q_g^{true}} \sim \chi^2_d.

    The correspondence with the classical result is

    s2↔qgresidual s^2 \longleftrightarrow q_g^{residual}

    and

    σ2↔qgtrue. \sigma^2 \longleftrightarrow q_g^{true}.

    Here, qgresidualq_g^{residual} is the observed noisy residual QL-dispersion estimate for gene gg, while qgtrueq_g^{true} is its unknown true value.

    The observed residual QL dispersion is obtained approximately from the residual negative-binomial deviance:

    qgresidual≈Dg,likelihoodd, q_g^{residual} \approx \frac{D_{g,\mathrm{likelihood}}}{d},

    where

    Dg,likelihood=2[ℓg(saturated)−ℓg(fitted)]. D_{g,\mathrm{likelihood}} = 2\left[ \ell_g(\mathrm{saturated}) - \ell_g(\mathrm{fitted}) \right].

    Thus Dg,likelihoodD_{g,\mathrm{likelihood}} measures residual lack-of-fit of the negative-binomial model, and dividing by the residual degrees of freedom produces the variance-like quantity qgresidualq_g^{residual}.

    The unknown true QL dispersion

    From

    dqgresidualqgtrue∼χd2, \frac{d\,q_g^{residual}} {q_g^{true}} \sim \chi^2_d,

    we cannot solve directly for qgtrueq_g^{true}.

    Algebraically,

    qgtrue=dqgresidualχd2, q_g^{true} = \frac{d\,q_g^{residual}} {\chi^2_d},

    but the realised value of the χd2\chi^2_d random variable is unknown. The equation therefore describes the sampling distribution of qgresidualq_g^{residual} conditional on the unknown qgtrueq_g^{true}.

    The empirical-Bayes model supplies the second level:

    qgtrue∼s0g2d0χd02, q_g^{true} \sim s_{0g}^2 \frac{d_0}{\chi^2_{d_0}},

    where s0g2s_{0g}^2 is the expected residual QL dispersion for a gene with the abundance of gene gg, and d0d_0 is the prior degrees of freedom.

    The trend s0g2s_{0g}^2 is estimated from the collection of observed residual QL dispersions:

    {q1residual,q2residual,…,qGresidual}→s0g2. \{ q_1^{residual}, q_2^{residual}, \ldots, q_G^{residual} \} \longrightarrow s_{0g}^2.

    The three quantities therefore have distinct meanings:

    • qgresidualq_g^{residual} is the noisy residual QL-dispersion estimate obtained from gene gg;
    • s0g2s_{0g}^2 is the expected residual QL dispersion from the across-gene abundance trend;
    • qgtrueq_g^{true} is the latent true residual QL dispersion of gene gg.

    The hierarchy is

    s0g2→qgtrue→qgresidual. s_{0g}^2 \longrightarrow q_g^{true} \longrightarrow q_g^{residual}.

    Joining the equations to estimate d0d_0

    At this stage:

    • qgresidualq_g^{residual} is observed/calculated for every gene;
    • s0g2s_{0g}^2 is estimated from the abundance trend;
    • dd is known from the experimental design;
    • d0d_0 is unknown;
    • qgtrueq_g^{true} is also unknown.

    The sampling model can be written as

    qgresidual=qgtrueχd2d. q_g^{residual} = q_g^{true} \frac{\chi^2_d}{d}.

    The prior model gives

    qgtrue=s0g2d0χd02. q_g^{true} = s_{0g}^2 \frac{d_0}{\chi^2_{d_0}}.

    Substitution eliminates the latent qgtrueq_g^{true}:

    qgresidual=s0g2d0χd02χd2d. q_g^{residual} = s_{0g}^2 \frac{d_0}{\chi^2_{d_0}} \frac{\chi^2_d}{d}.

    Therefore,

    qgresiduals0g2=χd2/dχd02/d0∼Fd,d0. \boxed{ \frac{q_g^{residual}} {s_{0g}^2} = \frac{\chi^2_d/d} {\chi^2_{d_0}/d_0} \sim F_{d,d_0}. }

    The FF distribution arises because the expression is a ratio of two independent chi-square random variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom.

    Across thousands of genes, edgeR has the observed ratios

    q1residuals012,q2residuals022,… \frac{q_1^{residual}}{s_{01}^2}, \frac{q_2^{residual}}{s_{02}^2}, \ldots

    and uses their distribution to estimate d0d_0.

    Equivalently, on the log scale, the variance of the residual QL dispersions can be decomposed into sampling variability and genuine across-gene variability. For equal residual degrees of freedom dd,

    Var[log(qgresiduals0g2)]=ψ′(d/2)+ψ′(d0/2). \mathrm{Var} \left[ \log \left( \frac{q_g^{residual}}{s_{0g}^2} \right) \right] = \psi'(d/2) + \psi'(d_0/2).

    The first term is determined by the known residual degrees of freedom dd. The remaining variation identifies d0d_0.

    A large d0d_0 means the true residual QL dispersions are tightly concentrated around their trend and supports stronger empirical-Bayes shrinkage. A small d0d_0 means greater genuine between-gene heterogeneity and supports weaker shrinkage.

    How d0d_0 is used for the negative-binomial dispersion

    The important distinction is that the QL hierarchy above is used to estimate the strength of shrinkage, d0d_0. It does not imply that edgeR places the same scaled-inverse-chi-square prior directly on its negative-binomial dispersion ϕg\phi_g.

    For the negative-binomial dispersion, edgeR instead combines the gene-specific and shared adjusted profile likelihoods using weighted likelihood. Conceptually,

    ϕtrend,g+gene-specific NB likelihood+d0→ϕtagwise,g. \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} + \text{gene-specific NB likelihood} + d_0 \longrightarrow \phi_{\mathrm{tagwise},g}.

    Thus:

    • ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} is the negative-binomial dispersion trend that brmDE uses as its prior location;
    • d0d_0 describes the empirical-Bayes shrinkage strength;
    • ϕtagwise,g\phi_{\mathrm{tagwise},g} is edgeR’s already-moderated gene-specific NB dispersion and is not passed to brmDE as a prior location.

    brmDE takes ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} and d0d_0 and translates them into the Gamma or Student-t prior constructions described above. The scaled-inverse-chi-square model applied directly to ϕg\phi_g is therefore a brmDE approximation used to construct that Bayesian prior.

    Appendix 2: Where edgeR’s dispersion and the brms shape differ

    The design. estimateDisp() fits a fixed-effects GLM, so a random-effect term has to be handled somehow, and the two available choices bias ϕg\phi_g in opposite directions. Stripping it, for example passing ~ dex while brms fits ~ dex + (1 | cell), leaves the between-cell variance nowhere to go but ϕg\phi_g, inflating it. Passing the fixed-effect analogue (~ dex + cell) estimates those cell effects without shrinkage, so they absorb more variance than the mixed model’s partially pooled ones will, leaving ϕg\phi_g below the conditional shape brms is going to estimate. The target sits between the two:

    ϕedgeR(∼dex+cell)≤ϕbrmsconditional≤ϕedgeR(∼dex), \phi^{(\sim\,\mathrm{dex}\,+\,\mathrm{cell})}_{\mathrm{edgeR}} \;\le\; \phi^{\mathrm{conditional}}_{\mathrm{brms}} \;\le\; \phi^{(\sim\,\mathrm{dex})}_{\mathrm{edgeR}},

    with the position depending on how hard the mixed model shrinks, which is not known before fitting.

    The fixed-effect analogue also costs residual degrees of freedom. On airway’s 8 samples, ~ dex + cell spans 5 columns and leaves d=3d=3, whereas ~ dex leaves d=6d=6. This reduction in residual degrees of freedom increases the sampling uncertainty of the gene-wise residual dispersion estimates and can therefore affect the empirically estimated d0d_0. Because the brmDE prior width is ultimately calibrated from d0d_0, the choice of fixed-effect approximation can indirectly change the prior width.

    The family. The default is zero-inflated negative binomial. shape there is the same parameter as in negbinomial(), with the same NB kernel and the same log link; what differs is the estimand. It describes the count component, whereas edgeR fits a plain negative binomial to the marginal counts.

    Zero inflation contributes overdispersion quadratic in μ\mu exactly as the NB dispersion does, so a marginal fit sees the two combined. Matching Var(Y)=E[Y]+ϕE[Y]2\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathrm{E}[Y] + \phi\,\mathrm{E}[Y]^2 against the zero-inflated moments gives

    ϕmarginal=ϕ+π1−π,π=𝚣𝚒, \phi_{\mathrm{marginal}} = \frac{\phi+\pi}{1-\pi}, \qquad \pi=\texttt{zi},

    which pins both the direction and the size of that mismatch. edgeR’s estimate exceeds the ZINB component’s ϕ\phi whenever π>0\pi>0, by roughly π\pi in absolute terms and π/ϕ\pi/\phi in relative terms, so genes with small dispersion are the most distorted. The same expression is why zi and shape are only weakly separated: the mean-variance relationship constrains the combination, not the pair, leaving the shape of the zero mass as the main information that distinguishes them.

    Which prior to use: rule of thumb

    • If you are fitting a mixed-effect model, a zero-inflated negative-binomial model, or any model that the frequentist dispersion estimator cannot fit directly, use the Student-t prior. Its heavier tails allow the data to deviate more easily from the upstream approximation when there is enough information.

    • If you are fitting a fixed-effect model that edgeR or DESeq2 can represent directly, using a negative-binomial distribution, and you place substantial trust in the upstream dispersion inference, use the Gamma prior.

    Appendix 3: Examples of how to approximate a mixed-effect model with a fixed-effect one

    edgeR and DESeq2 have no random effects. To obtain the most relevant dispersion estimate, we can approximate the model fitted in brmDE using its fixed-effect analogue: drop the | and promote the grouping factor to a fixed term. If the random term also has a slope, include the interaction.

    Mixed-effect model (brmDE) Fixed-effect analogue (estimate_dispersion())
    ~ treatment + (1 \| hospital) ~ treatment + hospital
    ~ treatment + (1 \| hospital) + (1 \| batch) ~ treatment + hospital + batch
    ~ treatment + (treatment \| hospital) ~ treatment * hospital

    The last row is the random-slope case: (treatment | hospital) is (1 + treatment | hospital), so the analogue needs hospital-specific intercepts and hospital-specific treatment effects, which is treatment * hospital.

    Do not expand a nested random intercept (1 | hospital/ward) as hospital / ward. That formula is hospital + hospital:ward, which is rank-deficient when every ward belongs to one hospital, and edgeR will not fit it. Use the innermost grouping instead, uniquely coded: ~ treatment + ward.
